questions.q: A note reads: 'a sticky (damp), sweltering (very hot) afternoon, a steady drizzle and a falling barometer.' Counting each element once, the note covers ___ of the five elements of weather.
A newsroom intern drafts four one-line bulletins for a hill town. Which line speaks about exactly one element of weather, with no second element slipping in?
questions.a: The pressure bulletin is the only line with a single element. The cold drizzle joins temperature and precipitation, the damp air with a stiff breeze joins humidity and wind, and hot and sticky afternoons join temperature and humidity.
o: Atmospheric pressure fell steeply between midnight and dawn.
A cold drizzle kept falling through the whole of the morning.
Damp air and a stiff breeze made the evening unpleasant.
Hot and sticky afternoons are likely to continue all week.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air above us, felt on the Earth's surface, so it is a different element from wind, which is the movement of air.
Statement 2: Precipitation covers only water that falls as rain; snow, sleet and hail belong to other elements.
Statement 3: A person who notes only how fast the air is moving has recorded just one feature of one element.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: precipitation is any form of water that falls from the sky, including snow, sleet and hail. Statement 1 is true (pressure is the weight of air, wind is its movement). Statement 3 is true: wind has two features, speed and direction, and speed alone is one of them.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A trekker's diary at 4,000 m reads: 'Entry 1: breathless and dizzy on the climb. Entry 2: the prayer flags hang absolutely still.' Which elements of weather do the two entries point to, in order?
questions.a: Breathlessness at height comes from lower atmospheric pressure, since the air is thinner and gives less oxygen. Flags hanging still say the wind speed is nil. Entry 1 is not wind, and Entry 2 is not pressure: still air is not low-pressure air.
o: Atmospheric pressure, then wind
Wind, then atmospheric pressure
Humidity, then wind
Atmospheric pressure, then temperature

questions.q:
A hill town's bulletins. Monday: 29 degrees Celsius, no rain, 1012 mb, wind 10 km/h from the west, humidity 45%. Tuesday: 29 degrees Celsius, no rain, 1004 mb, wind 25 km/h from the west, humidity 45%. Wednesday: 24 degrees Celsius, 12 mm of rain, 998 mb, wind 30 km/h from the north, humidity 85%.
(a) Between Monday and Tuesday exactly two elements changed. Name them.
(b) How many of the five elements changed between Tuesday and Wednesday? Name the feature of the wind that changed besides its speed.
questions.a: (a) Atmospheric pressure (1012 to 1004 mb) and wind (speed 10 to 25 km/h); temperature, precipitation and humidity stayed the same. (b) All five changed: temperature, precipitation, pressure, wind and humidity. Besides speed, the wind's direction changed from west to north.
s: Part (a): atmospheric pressure and wind
Part (b): all five elements; wind direction also changed

questions.q: True or False: A town's barometer reads 995 mb while the villages around it read 1010 mb. Because wind is the movement of air from low pressure to high pressure, air will flow out of the town towards the villages. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Wind is the movement of air from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, so air flows from the villages (1010 mb) into the town (995 mb), not out of it. The town is also below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: wind blows from high pressure to low pressure, so the air moves from the villages into the town

questions.q: A student models the lowest layer of the atmosphere at a scale of 1 cm for every 1.5 km. Her column for a tropical town is 12 cm tall. Using the chapter's range of 6 km to 18 km for the height of this layer, which pair is right: the height her column stands for, and the shortest column that still stays inside the range?
questions.a: 12 cm x 1.5 km = 18 km, the top of the chapter's range. The lower end, 6 km, needs 6 / 1.5 = 4 cm. The pair 8 km and 9 cm comes from dividing 12 by 1.5 and multiplying 6 by 1.5, the wrong way round both times. The pair 18 km and 6 cm reads the 6 km lower end as 6 cm without applying the scale. The pair 18 km and 9 cm multiplies the 6 km by 1.5 instead of dividing.
o: 18 km, and 4 cm
8 km, and 9 cm
18 km, and 6 cm
18 km, and 9 cm

questions.q: Imran says, 'When a cyclone is moving, atmospheric pressure is the dominant element, so a bulletin need not report the other four elements on that day.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that in different situations one of the elements is dominant, and it names atmospheric pressure when a cyclone is moving; dominant means it stands out, not that the others vanish. Temperature, precipitation, wind and humidity together with pressure define the weather at a place, so the bulletin still needs all five.
s: Verdict: No
Dominant means one element stands out in a situation; it is not the only one
The five elements together define the weather at a place

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A humid day need not be a rainy day.
Reason (R): Humidity is a measure of the water that is falling from the sky as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air, while water that falls from the sky is precipitation, so air can hold much vapour with nothing falling.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Rina says, 'Weather and atmosphere mean the same thing.'
(a) Using the chapter's definition, state how weather is related to the atmosphere.
(b) A coastal town records 26 degrees Celsius at 7 a.m. and 33 degrees Celsius at 3 p.m. on one day. Can these be two different weathers over the same atmosphere? Give the reason from the definition.
questions.a: (a) The atmosphere is the layer of gases (air) around the Earth; weather is the state of that atmosphere at a particular time and place. (b) Yes. Weather is tied to a particular time as well as a place, so the same town can have a different state of the atmosphere at 7 a.m. and at 3 p.m.
s: Part (a): weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular time and place
Part (b): yes, because weather belongs to a particular time, so it can differ at one place

questions.q: Kavya's weather card has three entries only: temperature, rainfall and wind (speed and direction). Judge whether the card is enough for each of three users. (i) A farmer who wants to guess from which side the rain may arrive. (ii) A coastal town watching a cyclone approach. (iii) A family deciding whether wet clothes will dry on the line by evening. Where it is not enough, say which element of the chapter must be added and why.
questions.a: (i) Enough: farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from, and the card gives wind direction. (ii) Not enough: atmospheric pressure must be added, because it is the dominant element when a cyclone moves and a fall below 1000 mb indicates a depression. (iii) Not enough: humidity must be added, because when the air already holds much water vapour, water evaporates slowly and clothes stay damp. (Part (iii) uses the humidity rule from the LET'S REMEMBER box on evaporation, which the book gives beside the elements.)
s: (i) wind is enough for the farmer: farmers use wind direction to predict where rain might come from
(ii) adds atmospheric pressure
(ii) reason: dominant with a cyclone; below 1000 mb is a depression
(iii) adds humidity
(iii) reason: much water vapour makes evaporation slow

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the element of weather that decides it in Column II.
Column I: 1. The air feels 'heavy' just before a thunderstorm   2. Seeds are carried across a field   3. Wet clothes stay damp on a rainy day because water evaporates slowly   4. Curd takes longer to set on a day that feels colder than usual
Column II: (a) Humidity   (b) Temperature   (c) Atmospheric pressure   (d) Wind
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: A 'heavy' feeling before a storm relates to atmospheric pressure (c); seeds flying are carried by wind (d); slow evaporation on a rainy day is a matter of humidity (a); slower setting of curd on a colder day points to temperature (b). The other pairings swap two of these.

questions.q:
A kite club's log for a windy afternoon reads only 'wind: 15 km/h'. A farmer who borrows the log wants to guess from which side the rain may arrive.
(a) Which feature of the wind is missing from the log?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why the farmer cannot use the log, and name one other kind of user who would be hurt by the same gap.
questions.a: (a) The direction of the wind; the log gives only speed. (b) The farmer uses wind direction to predict where rain might come from, so speed alone does not help. A pilot or a sailor would also be hurt, because the wind has a great influence on flying or sailing and they need to be aware of wind data.
s: Part (a): direction is missing
Part (b): farmers use direction to predict where rain may come from; a pilot or sailor also needs wind data

questions.q: A school logbook for one day has six entries: maximum 33 degrees Celsius, minimum 21 degrees Celsius, wind 15 km/h, wind from the west, 1005 mb, and 12 mm in the rain gauge. How many of the five elements of weather does the logbook cover, and which is missing?
questions.a: The two temperatures are one element (temperature), speed and direction are the two features of one element (wind), 1005 mb is atmospheric pressure and 12 mm is precipitation. That is four elements, and humidity is the one missing. Counting entries gives six, which is not the number of elements.
o: Four of the five; humidity is missing
Six of the five; each entry is an element
Five of the five; nothing is missing
Four of the five; atmospheric pressure is missing

questions.q: A student's chart for a town shows 'humidity: 70%' and nothing else. Show why this reading alone cannot tell us whether any precipitation is falling there.
questions.a: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air, while precipitation is water that falls from the sky as rain, snow, sleet or hail. They are two separate elements measured separately, so the vapour reading does not say whether anything is falling; the chart would also need a precipitation record such as a rain gauge reading.
s: Humidity is water vapour in the air
Precipitation is water that falls, a separate element
So a precipitation record is also needed

questions.q:
Ravi's log for a day in Shimla lists: 'morning: snow; noon: hail; dusk: drizzle; all day: relative humidity 80%'.
(a) How many of the four entries are forms of precipitation? Name them.
(b) Why does the humidity entry not belong with them, even though it is also about water?
questions.a: (a) Three: snow, hail and drizzle, all water falling from the sky. (b) Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; it does not fall, and so it is a separate element from precipitation.
s: Part (a): three, snow, hail and drizzle
Part (b): humidity is water vapour in the air, not water that falls

questions.q:
A school in Pune must decide at 6 a.m. whether the 4 p.m. annual-day rehearsal for 300 students is held on the open ground or in the hall, which seats only 120, so the cast would have to rehearse in three shifts. The principal wants the ground only if it will be dry by 4 p.m. The science club's morning notes read: 'A: 14 mm collected in the gauge between 9 p.m. and 5 a.m., when the rain stopped. B: wind 35 km/h from the west, forecast to ease to 10 km/h by noon. C: 24 degrees Celsius. D: relative humidity 78%; the sky is still overcast and the ground is still soggy.'
(a) Name the element of weather that each of the notes A to D records.
(b) In which band does note D fall, and what does that band and the easing of the wind do to the drying of the wet ground?
(c) Decide between the ground and the hall, and justify with at least two elements.
questions.a: (a) A precipitation, B wind, C temperature, D humidity. (b) 78% lies in the 60 to 80% band of humid weather, so water evaporates slowly; the chapter says a greater wind speed dries soil faster, so the wind easing from 35 to 10 km/h slows the drying further. Both effects make the ground dry slowly. (c) The hall, in three shifts: 14 mm fell until 5 a.m., only 11 hours before 4 p.m., the sky is overcast, the air is humid and the wind is easing, so the ground will probably still be soggy at 4 p.m.; the cost accepted is the three shifts. A choice of the ground does not earn the mark, because every reading points to slow drying and the principal's own condition (dry by 4 p.m.) is unlikely to be met.
s: Part (a): precipitation, wind, temperature, humidity
Part (b): humid band means slow evaporation, and the easing wind slows the drying of soil further
Part (c): the hall in three shifts, justified with two elements; the ground does not meet the principal's condition

questions.q:
The chapter says that in different situations one element of weather is dominant. For each news flash, name the dominant element and the reason in one line.
(i) A loo, a strong, hot, dusty wind, sweeps across north India in June.
(ii) The streets of a coastal city flood in July.
(iii) A May afternoon in Jaipur touches 44 degrees Celsius.
(iv) A forest fire is spreading across a hillside.
(v) Ravi says, 'Rainfall is dominant in July, so temperature, wind, pressure and humidity are not elements of July's weather at all.' Reply in one or two sentences.
questions.a: (i) Wind: the chapter gives a blowing loo as a case in which wind is dominant. (ii) Precipitation (rainfall): rainfall is dominant in July. (iii) Temperature: temperature is dominant in May. (iv) Wind: a spreading forest fire is the chapter's other case where wind is dominant. (v) Ravi is wrong. Dominant means one element stands out in a situation; temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind and humidity together still define the weather at a place.
s: (i) wind (loo)
(ii) precipitation in July
(iii) temperature in May
(iv) wind (spreading forest fire)
(v) dominant does not mean the only element; all five together define the weather

questions.q: Write three one-sentence entries for a school diary on a winter morning in Shimla: (i) one that records precipitation in a form other than rain, (ii) one that records humidity, and (iii) one that records wind using both of its features. Name the element after each.
questions.a: Any three correct sentences, for example: (i) 'Snow fell from 6 a.m.' (precipitation); (ii) 'The air is full of water vapour and clothes will not dry' (humidity); (iii) 'The wind blew at 15 km/h from the north' (wind: speed and direction).
s: Precipitation entry in a form other than rain, named
Humidity entry about water vapour in the air, named
Wind entry giving both speed and direction, named

questions.q:
On a May day in coastal Odisha a cyclone is moving up the Bay of Bengal. The port barometer read 1002 mb at 6 a.m. and 987 mb at 6 p.m.; the thermometer touched 41 degrees Celsius at noon; the wind at 6 p.m. blew at 60 km/h. A local radio station has 30 seconds for its evening bulletin, so the editor can lead with one element and must squeeze the rest into a closing line.
(a) By how many millibars did the pressure fall in the 12 hours, and what is the average fall per hour?
(b) Is 987 mb a depression by the chapter's rule, what can such a system become, and which element does the chapter name as dominant when a cyclone is moving (and which in May)?
(c) Which element should the editor lead with? Decide and justify with the readings.
questions.a: (a) 1002 - 987 = 15 mb, an average of 15 / 12 = 1.25 mb per hour. (b) Yes: a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression, which can develop into a storm or a cyclone. Atmospheric pressure is dominant while a cyclone is moving; temperature is dominant in May. (c) Lead with atmospheric pressure: the steady fall to 987 mb is the warning of the cyclone for which the coast must prepare, whereas the 41 degrees is a reading people already feel and gives no warning. A lead with temperature does not earn the mark, because the cyclone is moving and the fall is below the depression mark.
s: Part (a): 15 mb; 1.25 mb per hour
Part (b): yes, below 1000 mb; storm or cyclone; pressure dominant with a cyclone, temperature in May
Part (c): lead with pressure, justified with the readings

questions.q: A student's project says, 'Once instruments arrived, nature's signs stopped being used for weather.' A survey of villages finds four things. Which finding most directly contradicts her claim?
questions.a: Elders who still use ants carrying their eggs uphill to decide on sowing before the monsoon show that nature's signs are still in use, which is what the chapter says about the monsoon. A district gauge, a school thermometer and a pine cone closing in humid air are all true, but none of them shows people still using signs to predict.
o: Elders in a Konkan village still watch ants carrying eggs uphill to decide when to sow before the monsoon.
A district office records the rainfall of every day with a rain gauge.
A school science club keeps a thermometer on the verandah wall.
Pine cones in a hill garden close when the air turns humid.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A prediction made from the opening and closing of pine cones is meteorology, the systematic study of weather and its evolution.
Statement 2: The knowledge of reading nature's signs has been passed down from generation to generation.
Statement 3: Celsius and Fahrenheit are two scales for one temperature, so a reading of 15 on one scale is also 15 on the other.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: reading pine cones is a traditional way of reading nature's signals, while meteorology is the systematic study of weather and the basis of forecasting. Statement 3 is false: 15 degrees Celsius is the same as 59 degrees Fahrenheit, so the numbers differ across the scales. Statement 2 is in the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with what it indicates in Column II.
Column I: 1. Ants shifting their eggs to higher ground   2. Pine cones tightly shut   3. Pine cones wide open   4. The systematic study of weather and its evolution, the basis of forecasting
Column II: (a) Dry conditions   (b) Meteorology   (c) Humid conditions   (d) Heavy rain is expected
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Ants moving their eggs uphill is a natural behaviour that indicates a coming change in weather, especially heavy rain (d). Pine cones close in humid conditions (c) and open in dry conditions (a). The chapter's glossary defines meteorology as the systematic study of weather and its evolution, the basis for weather forecasting (b). The other pairings swap the two pine-cone states or the ants and the study of weather.

questions.q: Dattu logs what he sees over six evenings. Evening 1: ants carrying eggs uphill and frogs croaking loudly. Evening 2: nothing unusual. Evening 3: birds flying low. Evening 4: pine cones shut, squirrels gathering nuts and frogs croaking loudly. Evening 5: a thermometer reading of 31 degrees Celsius and a rain gauge reading of 2 mm. Evening 6: 'it feels chilly'. The number of sightings that are nature's signs of the kind the chapter lists is ___.

Krishnan in Chennai says, 'It is 20 degrees Celsius here and I feel a little cold.' Amir in Kashmir says, 'My old thermometer shows 55 degrees Fahrenheit and it is quite pleasant.' Use the chapter's pair 15 degrees Celsius = 59 degrees Fahrenheit.
(a) Whose place is warmer?
(b) Why do their feelings not settle the question?
questions.a: (a) Chennai. 55 degrees Fahrenheit is lower than 59 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 15 degrees Celsius, and 15 is lower than Krishnan's 20 degrees Celsius. (b) What is cold for one person may be quite pleasant for another, so feelings differ and cannot be compared; readings put on one scale can.
s: Part (a): Chennai is warmer, by converting through 59 F = 15 C
Part (b): feelings differ between people, so readings on one scale are compared

questions.q: A village school wants a 'monsoon watch' board. The headmaster says it must use the signs the elders trust, yet it must also let the school compare its weather with that of another village. Draw up a plan for the board using the chapter, and say what the board can and cannot tell.
questions.a: The board names at least two signs from the chapter, such as ants carrying eggs to higher ground, frogs croaking loudly, birds flying low or pine cones opening and closing, with the coming weather each points to (rain or storms; pine cones close in humid and open in dry conditions). For comparison it adds a measured reading, for example a thermometer reading on a named scale, because feelings differ between people and only readings on an agreed scale can be compared across places. It admits that the signs only indicate coming rain and give no number. It sets beside them a forecast from meteorology, the systematic study of weather and the basis of forecasting.
s: Names at least two signs with what each points to
Adds a measured reading on a named, agreed scale for comparison
Reason: feelings differ, so only agreed-scale readings compare places
States what the signs cannot tell: they give no number, only an indication
Sets a forecast from meteorology beside the signs, as the basis of forecasting

questions.q: True or False: Meteorologists can predict the weather only a few hours ahead; for days or weeks ahead, only traditional signs are available. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that meteorologists use precise measurements to try to predict how the weather will behave in a region after a few hours, a few days or even a few weeks. Traditional signs are an older, passed-down way, not the only one beyond a few hours.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: meteorologists predict hours, days or even weeks ahead from measured data

questions.q: By his notes, Dattu's saying 'when the ants carry their eggs uphill, heavy rain follows' has held in 9 of the last 10 monsoons. Which statement about the saying is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Ants shifting their eggs to higher ground is a natural behaviour that indicates a coming change in weather, and such knowledge is handed down and still used. Meteorology is systematic measurement; the saying gives no number on a common scale. The chapter links humidity to pine cones, not ants, and it says traditional ways are still in use.
o: A valuable inherited hint of coming rain, but not a reading another place can compare
It counts as meteorology, because it has been checked against the rains for many years
It must be false, because the chapter says instruments have replaced traditional ways
It is a humidity reading, because ants respond to the humidity of the air just as pine cones do

questions.q: Nisha says, 'A pine cone that has snapped shut tells us that rain is falling at that very moment.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that a shut cone is a sign about the air: pine cones close in humid conditions to protect their seeds. She is wrong to say it means rain is falling now: the cone responds to the humidity of the air, and humid air does not by itself mean that water is falling from the sky; precipitation is a separate element.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: cones close in humid conditions, so a shut cone says the air is humid
What is wrong: the cone follows humidity, not falling rain; precipitation is a separate element

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two farmers in different states, each watching ants carry their eggs uphill, cannot tell from the ants alone whose rain will be heavier.
Reason (R): A natural sign gives an indication of coming rain, but no number on a commonly agreed scale.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. The ants point to coming (heavy) rain, but they give no amount that can be put side by side with another place, since that needs a measurement on a common scale.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
At 7 a.m. the school gardener finds the nursery's pine cones wide open, while the ants are already shifting their eggs uphill and the frogs by the tank are very loud. The gardener reads the cones only for the state of the air at that moment. A student says the signs contradict one another.
(a) What do the open pine cones say about the air at that moment?
(b) What do the ants and frogs say about the days ahead, and is the student right that the signs contradict?
questions.a: (a) Pine cones open in dry conditions, so the air around them at that moment is dry. (b) The ants and frogs point to expected rain, especially heavy rain. The student is not right: the cones respond to the humidity of the air now, while the ants and frogs warn of a change in weather to come, so they speak of different times.
s: Part (a): open cones mean dry air at present
Part (b): ants and frogs point to coming rain; the signs are about different times, so no contradiction

questions.q:
A farmer near Nashik has 5 acres of paddy ready to cut. His father notes that the ants in the yard are carrying their eggs to a high shelf, that the frogs by the well are very loud, and that the pine cones on the roadside trees are shut. The radio forecast, made from measured data, says the next three days will be dry. Cutting now costs 4,000 rupees an acre in hired labour. Cut paddy that lies in the field when it rains loses 10,000 rupees an acre. A tarpaulin to cover the cut paddy costs 1,500 rupees an acre. Waiting three days would raise the labour cost to 7,000 rupees an acre.
(a) Which of the three observations is driven by humidity, and what does it suggest about the air?
(b) Find the total cost of each plan: cut now and cover; cut now without cover (if no rain comes, and if rain comes); wait three days and cut.
(c) Decide among the plans, saying what chance of rain would make the cover worth buying.
questions.a: (a) The shut pine cones; they close in humid conditions, so the air is humid. (b) Cut and cover: 5 x (4,000 + 1,500) = 27,500 rupees. Cut without cover: 5 x 4,000 = 20,000 rupees if no rain, 20,000 + 5 x 10,000 = 70,000 rupees if rain falls on the cut paddy. Wait: 5 x 7,000 = 35,000 rupees. (c) Waiting is the dearest plan, so it is out. The cover costs 7,500 rupees more than no cover and saves 50,000 if it rains, so it pays when the chance of rain on the cut paddy is above 7,500 / 50,000 = 15 per cent. Cut now and cover is supported: three signs point to rain, and a forecast from measured data is precise but not certain, so a 15 per cent chance is easy to believe. Cutting without cover earns the mark only if it argues that the chance is below 15 per cent and says why (the forecast of three dry days).
s: Part (a): the shut pine cones; humid air
Part (c): decision using the 15 per cent break-even, weighing the signs against the forecast

questions.q: The gardener of a school notes that the pine cones in the nursery were wide open at 8 a.m. and tightly shut by 4 p.m. on the same day. What does this suggest about the air around them during the day?
questions.a: Pine cones open in dry conditions to release their seeds and close in humid conditions to protect them. Open at 8 a.m. points to dry air and shut at 4 p.m. to humid air, so humidity rose. They are driven by humidity, not at random.
o: Its humidity rose between morning and afternoon
Its humidity fell between morning and afternoon
It was humid at both times, since pine cones move at random
Its temperature changed, which says nothing about humidity

questions.q:
A school must cancel its hired tent at least 48 hours before any expected rain on its Thursday sports day. A meteorologist's forecast issued at 9 a.m. on Monday says heavy rain is expected from 6 a.m. on Thursday. On Wednesday at 6 p.m. the school gardener sees ants carrying their eggs uphill.
(a) How many hours before the rain does the forecast reach the school, and how many hours before the rain does the gardener's sign appear?
(b) Which of the two lets the school cancel in time, and what is the limit of the sign?
questions.a: (a) Monday 9 a.m. to Thursday 6 a.m. is 72 - 3 = 69 hours; Wednesday 6 p.m. to Thursday 6 a.m. is 12 hours. (b) The forecast: 69 hours is more than the 48 hours needed, while 12 hours is less. The ants are a valuable sign that heavy rain may come, but they give no amount and no time on a measured scale, whereas meteorology studies the weather systematically and forecasts hours or days ahead.
s: Part (a): 69 hours and 12 hours
Part (b): the forecast (69 is above 48, 12 is below); the sign gives only an indication, with no measured amount or time

questions.q: Dattu says, 'The frogs are loud tonight, so tomorrow it will rain exactly 40 mm.' Show why none of the nature's signs in the chapter can support the number 40 mm.
questions.a: The signs in the chapter, such as croaking frogs, ants shifting eggs or low-flying birds, only point to coming rain or storms; they say that rain may come, not how much. An amount can be stated only by measuring it with an instrument on an agreed unit, which the signs do not provide, so 40 mm cannot be read from the frogs.
s: Signs only indicate coming rain or storms
An amount needs measurement with an instrument
A number needs an agreed unit that others can compare

questions.q: Dattu has watched ants and frogs for forty years and is right about the rains most years. Asha has spent two years recording temperature, rainfall and pressure at set times every day and now uses the figures to forecast the next few days. Which of the two is practising meteorology, as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: Meteorology is the systematic study of weather and its evolution, the basis for forecasting. Asha measures at set times and forecasts from her data. Dattu's knowledge is valuable, passed-down observation of nature, but it is not measurement. The chapter does not make a weather station a condition.
o: Asha, because she measures the weather systematically and forecasts from her data
Dattu, because forty years of watching is a longer study than two years of readings
Both, because anyone who predicts rain correctly is a meteorologist
Neither, because meteorology needs a weather station with an automatic instrument

questions.q:
While collecting sayings from an elder, a student writes down: 'When the pine cones snap shut, the washing will stay damp.'
(a) Which element of weather does the saying depend on?
(b) Does the saying agree with the chapter? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Humidity: pine cones are driven by environmental humidity. (b) Yes. Pine cones close in humid conditions, and when the amount of water in the air is high, water evaporates slowly, so washing stays damp.
s: Part (a): humidity
Part (b): cones close in humid air and evaporation is slow in humid air, so it agrees

questions.q: A student says, 'Instrument forecasts are scientific, so the elders' sayings about the weather are worthless.' Write a reasoned reply using the chapter.
questions.a: Birds flying low, ants carrying eggs, frogs croaking and pine cones gave valuable information about coming rain or storms. The knowledge has been passed down and in many parts of India is still used, especially for the monsoon. But a saying gives no reading on a commonly agreed scale, so places cannot be compared, and feelings of cold differ between people. Meteorology is the systematic study of weather, based on precise measurement, and it is the basis of forecasting. A balanced conclusion is expected; accept any sensible one, such as using sayings as a first hint to be checked against measured data.
s: Sayings gave valuable information on rain or storms
They are still used today, for example for the monsoon
They cannot give a comparable reading on an agreed scale
Meteorology adds precise measurement and forecasting
A balanced conclusion (accept any sensible one)

questions.q:
Lakshmi in Chennai writes that her morning felt chilly and that her thermometer, marked in degrees Celsius, shows 15. Harpreet in Leh writes that his morning felt pleasant and that his old thermometer, which has only the Fahrenheit scale, shows 59. Their cousin Neha in Pune measured 18 degrees Celsius and found it warm. They plan a joint trek and want a single thermometer for the group. The trek leader's rule is that every member must be able to read the group thermometer without converting, and Harpreet has only ever used the Fahrenheit scale: one marked only in Celsius costs 250 rupees, and one marked in both scales costs 400 rupees.
(a) Which of the three readings can be compared with another as they stand, with no conversion?
(b) Write Harpreet's reading in Celsius.
(c) Whose mornings were equally cold, and what does this show about the words chilly and pleasant?
(d) Which thermometer should the group buy? Decide and justify, using the leader's rule and the prices.
questions.a: (a) Lakshmi's 15 degrees Celsius and Neha's 18 degrees Celsius, because both are on the same scale; Harpreet's is on a different one. (b) 15 degrees Celsius, since 59 degrees Fahrenheit is the same as 15 degrees Celsius. (c) Lakshmi's and Harpreet's mornings, both 15 degrees Celsius, although she called hers chilly and he called his pleasant, so such words are feelings that differ between people. (d) The two-scale thermometer at 400 rupees: only it lets Harpreet read his own scale and the others read Celsius, so the leader's rule is met, for 150 rupees more. The Celsius-only thermometer at 250 rupees saves 150 rupees but breaks the rule for Harpreet; an answer that chooses it earns 1 of the 2 marks only if it correctly names the saving of 150 rupees and admits that Harpreet would have to convert.
s: Parts (a) and (b): the two Celsius readings; 15 degrees Celsius
Part (c): Lakshmi and Harpreet; feelings differ for the same temperature
Part (d): two-scale thermometer, justified by the leader's rule and the 150 rupees extra (2); Celsius-only with the saving named and the conversion burden admitted (1)

questions.q: Write a three-line phone call in which Krishnan in Chennai and Amir in Kashmir exchange temperatures so that each understands the other exactly. One of them must use the Celsius scale and the other the Fahrenheit scale, and the call must use the chapter's pair of equal readings.
questions.a: For example: Krishnan: 'It is 15 degrees Celsius in Chennai.' Amir: 'My thermometer shows 59 degrees Fahrenheit here.' Krishnan: 'Then we have the same temperature, since 15 degrees Celsius is 59 degrees Fahrenheit.' The call names the scale with each number and uses the pair correctly.
s: Krishnan states a reading with its scale (Celsius)
Amir states a reading with its scale (Fahrenheit)
Uses 15 degrees Celsius = 59 degrees Fahrenheit correctly to compare

questions.q: A recording thermometer in Ajmer gave a maximum of 41 and a minimum of 23 degrees Celsius for one day. The next day the range was 4 degrees more than this day's range, and the minimum was 3 degrees lower than this day's minimum. What was the next day's maximum, in degrees Celsius?
questions.a: This day's range is 41 - 23 = 18, so the next day's range is 22. The next minimum is 23 - 3 = 20. The maximum is 20 + 22 = 42. Keeping the old minimum gives 45, using the old range with the new minimum gives 38, and moving the minimum the wrong way gives 48.

questions.q: True or False: For any day, the range of temperature equals twice the difference between the maximum temperature and the mean daily temperature. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The mean (maximum + minimum) divided by 2 lies exactly halfway between the two, so maximum minus mean is half of (maximum minus minimum). Doubling it gives the range. Check: maximum 34, minimum 18, mean 26, 2 x (34 - 26) = 16 = range.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the mean lies halfway between maximum and minimum, so maximum minus mean is half the range

questions.q: Radha's chart entry for a day in Bhopal reads: maximum 38 degrees Celsius, minimum 41 degrees Celsius. She works out the mean as 39.5. What should her teacher conclude?
questions.a: The maximum is the highest and the minimum the lowest temperature of the period, so the maximum cannot be lower than the minimum. The entry has been swapped or wrongly recorded; the range would come out negative (38 - 41 = -3), which is impossible, and a mean between two swapped values hides the error.
o: The two readings were swapped or wrongly recorded, since a day's maximum cannot be below its minimum
The range of the day was 3 degrees Celsius and the entry is acceptable, because range is the difference of the readings
The entry is fine, because the mean of 39.5 lies between 38 and 41
The thermometer must be digital, as only a digital one can show a minimum above the maximum

questions.q:
A school records (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius on three days: (36, 22), (38, 24) and (37, 21).
(a) Find the range of temperature for the whole three-day period.
(b) A student adds the three daily ranges and gets 44. Explain why this cannot be the range for the period.
questions.a: (a) The highest maximum is 38 and the lowest minimum is 21, so the range is 38 - 21 = 17. (b) The range of a period is the highest maximum minus the lowest minimum over that period; the three daily ranges (14, 14 and 16) each cover only their own day, so adding them overcounts. The period's range cannot exceed the gap between the hottest and the coldest reading of all.
s: Part (b): period range is highest maximum minus lowest minimum, not a sum of daily ranges

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The range of temperature for a day can be found from a thermometer that shows only the temperature at the moment of reading.
Statement 2: A day with a maximum of 34 and a minimum of 18 degrees Celsius has a mean daily temperature of 26 degrees Celsius.
Statement 3: If a day's maximum is 4 degrees higher than it was while its minimum is unchanged, the range rises by 4 degrees and the mean daily temperature rises by 2 degrees.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the range needs the day's maximum and minimum, and an ambient thermometer shows only one reading. Statement 2 is true: (34 + 18)/2 = 26. Statement 3 is true: the range is the maximum minus the minimum, so it rises by 4, and the mean is the sum divided by 2, so it rises by 4/2 = 2.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A day's register gives a range of 15 and a mean daily temperature of 27 degrees Celsius, but the maximum was copied as 36. The copied maximum is ___ degrees Celsius too high to fit the range and the mean.
A report gives a maximum of 36 and a minimum of 24 degrees Celsius for Nagpur. Meena writes the mean daily temperature as 12. What is the right mean, and what did she most probably find instead?
questions.a: The mean is (36 + 24) divided by 2 = 30. Her 12 is 36 - 24, the range. Halving the range would give 6, not 12, and 60 is the sum of the two readings.
o: 30 degrees Celsius; she found the range
30 degrees Celsius; she halved the range
60 degrees Celsius; she found the range
6 degrees Celsius; she found the range

questions.q: Sheela says, 'The mean daily temperature of a day can never be lower than that day's minimum or higher than its maximum.' Test her claim with Day A (maximum 30, minimum 16) and Day B (maximum 36, minimum 30).
questions.a: Yes, the claim holds. Day A: mean (30 + 16)/2 = 23, between 16 and 30. Day B: mean (36 + 30)/2 = 33, between 30 and 36. The mean is the value halfway between the maximum and the minimum, so it always lies between them.
s: Computes Day A mean 23 and checks it lies between 16 and 30
Computes Day B mean 33 and checks it lies between 30 and 36
Verdict: the claim is right, as the mean is halfway between the two

questions.q:
Kiran read her thermometer once at 9 a.m. (24 degrees Celsius) and once at 6 p.m. (28 degrees Celsius), and wrote: 'mean 26, range 4'. The day's recording thermometer showed a maximum of 33 and a minimum of 21 degrees Celsius.
(a) Find the day's true mean and range.
(b) Give the reason why her two readings gave a different range.
questions.a: (a) Mean (33 + 21)/2 = 27 degrees Celsius; range 33 - 21 = 12 degrees Celsius. (b) The range and the mean need the day's highest and lowest temperatures; her two spot readings were not necessarily taken at those moments, so they missed the extremes.
s: Part (a): mean 27 and range 12
Part (b): two spot readings miss the day's maximum and minimum

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The mean daily temperature is half of the difference between the maximum and the minimum.
Reason (R): The range of temperature is the maximum temperature minus the minimum temperature.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the mean is (maximum + minimum) divided by 2, not half of their difference. R is a true definition of range, so A is false and R is true.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

questions.q:
A city's chart for seven days gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius: (29, 16), (30, 15), (31, 17), (32, 18), (30, 17), (28, 14), (29, 15).
(i) Find the day with the greatest daily range, and that range.
(ii) On how many days did the mean daily temperature exceed 23 degrees Celsius?
(iii) Find the range for the whole week.
(iv) Find the day with the highest mean daily temperature and say what its range was.
(v) The daily means stay between 21 and 25, yet the weekly range is large. Explain what each number tells us.
questions.a: (i) Daily ranges are 13, 15, 14, 14, 13, 14, 14, so the second day has the greatest, 15. (ii) Means are 22.5, 22.5, 24, 25, 23.5, 21 and 22, so three days exceed 23 (the third, fourth and fifth). (iii) 32 - 14 = 18. (iv) The fourth day, mean 25, with a range of 14. (v) The means lie within a spread of only 4 degrees, so the typical level of the days is steady; the weekly range of 18 shows how far the hottest and coldest readings of the week are apart, which the means hide.
s: (i) second day, 15
(ii) three days
(iii) 18
(iv) fourth day, mean 25, range 14
(v) means steady, range shows the swing between extremes

questions.q: Use this week's chart: maximum temperatures 35, 33, 36, 34, 32, 37, 33 and minimum temperatures 24, 21, 26, 22, 20, 25, 23 degrees Celsius for seven days in order. Which day had the lowest mean daily temperature, and what was it?
questions.a: Daily means are 29.5, 27, 31, 28, 26, 31 and 28. The lowest is 26 on the fifth day, (32 + 20) divided by 2. The lowest minimum, 20, is not a mean.
o: The fifth day, 26 degrees Celsius
The fifth day, 20 degrees Celsius
The second day, 27 degrees Celsius
The fourth day, 28 degrees Celsius

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. Mean daily temperature of a day with maximum 32 and minimum 20 degrees Celsius   2. Minimum of a day whose maximum is 30 and whose range is 12 degrees Celsius   3. Maximum of a day whose mean is 25 and whose minimum is 19 degrees Celsius   4. Range of a day with maximum 33 and minimum 18 degrees Celsius
Column II: (a) 18   (b) 26   (c) 31   (d) 15
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: (1) (32 + 20)/2 = 26, so b. (2) 30 - 12 = 18, so a. (3) the sum of maximum and minimum is 2 x 25 = 50, so the maximum is 50 - 19 = 31, so c. (4) 33 - 18 = 15, so d. The other pairings swap two of these values.

questions.q:
(a) The India Meteorological Department was set up in 1875. How many years had it existed by 2025?
(b) In a coloured-liquid thermometer the liquid stands 3 cm up the tube in a cool hall and 5 cm up on a sunny verandah. Which place is warmer, and what does the liquid do as the temperature rises?
questions.a: (a) 2025 - 1875 = 150 years. (b) The verandah is warmer: the coloured liquid expands when the temperature increases, so its column rises higher in the tube.
s: Part (a): 150 years
Part (b): the verandah; the liquid expands as temperature rises

questions.q: A weather chart shows a day with a range of 12 degrees Celsius and a mean daily temperature of 24 degrees Celsius. Find the maximum and the minimum temperature of that day and verify your answer.
questions.a: Maximum + minimum = 2 x 24 = 48 and maximum - minimum = 12, so the maximum is 30 and the minimum is 18. Check: range 12, mean (30 + 18)/2 = 24.
s: Sets up sum 48 and difference 12
Maximum 30 and minimum 18
Verifies both range and mean

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Indore has 800 rupees to buy thermometers for the school roof. Thermometer P has a coloured liquid that rises in a thin tube, shows only the temperature at the moment it is read, and costs 180 rupees. Thermometer Q is digital, records the maximum and minimum of each day, is more precise, and costs 650 rupees. The club's aim is to report the range and the mean of every day for a month. The teacher would also like to know whether the four roof corners differ in temperature.
(a) Which thermometer can give the range of a day, and why can the other not do so on its own?
(b) Find the cost of one Q with one P, and of four P, and say whether each fits within 800 rupees and whether it can give a day's range and mean.
(c) Decide what the club should buy and justify.
questions.a: (a) Thermometer Q: the range needs the day's maximum and minimum, which it records; P shows only the present temperature. (b) One Q and one P: 650 + 180 = 830 rupees, which is 30 rupees over the 800. Four P: 4 x 180 = 720 rupees, which fits, but P records no maximum or minimum, so four P cannot give any day's range or mean. (c) Buy Q alone (650 rupees, 150 to spare): it is the only choice that meets the stated aim within the money. Four P do not earn the mark, because they fit the budget but cannot give the range and mean the club set out to report; the corner question can wait for a later purchase.
s: Part (a): Q records the day's maximum and minimum; P shows only the present temperature
Part (b): 830 rupees (30 over); 720 rupees (fits but no range or mean)
Part (c): Q alone, tied to the stated aim; four P do not meet it

questions.q:
A thermometer on a winter day shows a maximum of 22 and a minimum of 6 degrees Celsius.
(a) Find the range and the mean daily temperature.
(b) The thermometer is later found to read 2 degrees too high at both ends. Say what happens to the range and to the mean when the readings are corrected, with the new values.
questions.a: (a) Range 16, mean 14. (b) Corrected readings are 20 and 4: the range stays 16 because both ends move equally, while the mean falls by 2 to 12 degrees Celsius.
s: Part (a): range 16 and mean 14
Part (b): range unchanged at 16, mean 12

questions.q: Two days in Kota had the following readings: on Day P the maximum was 27 and the minimum 17 degrees Celsius; on Day Q the maximum was 33 and the minimum 11 degrees Celsius. Find the range and the mean daily temperature for each. Then say which day had the colder early morning and which statistic shows it, and justify the statement that 'the mean alone does not describe a day's temperature'.
questions.a: Day P: range 10, mean 22. Day Q: range 22, mean 22. The means are equal, yet Day Q was colder in the early morning: its minimum of 11 is below Day P's 17, and its range shows a wide swing. Hence the mean alone does not describe a day; the minimum or the range must be given too.
s: Day P range 10 and mean 22
Day Q range 22 and mean 22
Notes the means are equal
Day Q colder in the early morning: minimum 11 against 17
Conclusion: the mean hides the swing; range or minimum is also needed

questions.q: A hill station's chart gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius for four days: Monday (14, 6), Tuesday (16, 10), Wednesday (12, 4), Thursday (19, 8). Find (i) the day with the highest mean daily temperature and that mean, (ii) the day with the smallest range and that range, and (iii) the maximum and the range of a fifth day, Friday, whose minimum is 9 degrees Celsius and whose mean equals Thursday's.
questions.a: (i) Means are 10, 13, 8 and 13.5, so Thursday has the highest, 13.5 degrees Celsius. (ii) Ranges are 8, 6, 8 and 11, so Tuesday has the smallest, 6 degrees. (iii) Friday's maximum plus 9 is 2 x 13.5 = 27, so the maximum is 18 and the range is 18 - 9 = 9 degrees Celsius.
s: (i) Thursday, mean 13.5
(ii) Tuesday, range 6
(iii) maximum 18, range 9

questions.q:
A school in Pune plans its sports day, with races running from the morning chill into the afternoon. The weather chart for five days gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius: Day 1 (31, 19), Day 2 (33, 20), Day 3 (31, 21), Day 4 (34, 18), Day 5 (30, 22). The PT teacher wants the day with the lowest mean daily temperature. The school nurse wants the day on which the temperature changes least, and each is ready to defend a different day. The head decides that the youngest runners' health comes first: the day chosen must be the one with the smallest daily range, and the mean is used only to break a tie.
(a) Which day had the greatest range, and what was it?
(b) Find the mean daily temperature of every day and name the day with the lowest.
(c) What is the range of temperature for the whole five-day period?
(d) Which day should the school choose? Decide, name the statistic you rely on and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) Day 4, with a range of 34 - 18 = 16. (b) Means are 25, 26.5, 26, 26 and 26, so Day 1 has the lowest, 25 degrees Celsius. (c) Highest maximum 34, lowest minimum 18: range 16. (d) Day 5. By the head's rule the daily range decides: the ranges are 12, 13, 10, 16 and 8, so Day 5, with a range of 8, is the only day that meets it; what is given up is the lowest mean (26 against Day 1's 25 degrees Celsius). Choosing Day 1 on the lowest mean earns 1 of the 2 marks only if the answer admits that Day 1's range of 12 breaks the head's rule.
s: Parts (a) and (c): Day 4, range 16; five-day range 16
Part (b): means 25, 26.5, 26, 26, 26; Day 1 lowest
Part (d): Day 5 by the smallest-range rule, with the daily ranges and the cost (lowest mean) named (2); Day 1 with its range of 12 admitted as breaking the rule (1)

questions.q: On a coastal plain a barometer falls from 1012 mb at noon to 996 mb by evening, and Aditi says the air feels 'heavy', as it does before a thunderstorm. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter ties the 'heavy' feeling before a thunderstorm to atmospheric pressure, and a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression that can develop into a storm. A heavy feeling does not mean the pressure has risen: on the coast it sometimes drops dramatically. Humidity is not the chapter's explanation for the feeling, and 996 mb is not a mountain-style thinning of the air at sea level.
o: The feeling is linked to atmospheric pressure, and 996 mb is below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression that can become a storm
The feeling is linked to humidity, and 996 mb is an ordinary coastal reading
The feeling shows the weight of air has risen, so a heavy feeling means high pressure and clear weather
The fall to 996 mb shows the air has thinned as on a mountain, so a storm is impossible

questions.q: A hill walk starts at a coastal trailhead where the barometer reads the sea-coast normal of 1013 mb. Suppose the reading falls by 25 mb for every 300 m climbed. At a camp 1,500 m above the trailhead the barometer should read ___ mb.
A student's log for a wet evening reads: 'Rainfall 1004 mb; atmospheric pressure 16 mm.' Her teacher says the two entries have been swapped. What does the chapter let the teacher say?
questions.a: Rainfall is the depth of water collected in the cylinder of a rain gauge, measured in mm, so 16 mm is the rainfall; atmospheric pressure is read on a barometer in millibars, so 1004 mb is the pressure. The entries carry each other's units. The log is not right as it stands, and a heavy shower does not turn a depth into millibars.
o: Rainfall is a depth in mm from a rain gauge and pressure is in mb from a barometer, so the readings belong the other way round
The log is right, since both a rain gauge and a barometer give a depth of something collected
Only the pressure entry is wrong, since a barometer reads in mm and a rain gauge in mb
Both entries are right, since during heavy rain the rain gauge reads in millibars

questions.q:
On a calm day a hill station's barometer reads far lower than the barometer at a coastal town, which reads 1011 mb.
(a) Does the lower hill reading by itself show a depression? Say why it is lower.
(b) Next day the coastal barometer falls to 994 mb while the hill station's reading is unchanged. Which station's reading needs watching, and why?
questions.a: (a) No; a depression is a dramatic drop in pressure, whereas the hill station is higher up, where the air is thinner and presses less, so its reading is lower as a steady feature of the place. (b) The coastal town: a fall from about 1011 to 994 mb is a drop at a place whose normal is around 1013 mb, and below 1000 mb indicates a depression that can become a storm. The hill reading has not changed.
s: Part (a): no; thinner air at height gives a lower reading, not a depression
Part (b): the coastal town, since its fall to below 1000 mb indicates a depression; the hill reading is unchanged

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A rain gauge whose cylinder holds water 12 mm deep shows that the area received 12 mm of rainfall.
Statement 2: The atmospheric pressure on the plains or the coast is not always high; it can sometimes drop dramatically.
Statement 3: The air on a high mountain is thinner than on the plains below, so each breath brings less oxygen to the lungs.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. The depth of water collected is the rainfall; the chapter says pressure on the plains and the coast can drop dramatically; and the air on a mountain is thinner, with less oxygen available for the lungs.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: An air-ambulance doctor from the coast is flown to the army post at Khardung La and must start treating a patient on arrival, with no time for the pauses that trekkers are advised to take. Using only the chapter, say what she can expect, why, and what the chapter does not let you tell her.
questions.a: The coast's normal pressure is around 1013 mb and the post's is generally about 650 mb, so the air she breathes is much thinner. Thinner air means less oxygen reaches her lungs and blood, so her body works harder. She can therefore expect to feel breathless, dizzy or tired while working. Travellers are advised to pause to let the body acclimatise, and she will have had no pause, so she should expect these effects more. The chapter does not say how long acclimatising takes or how to treat the effects, so no number of hours or remedy can be given from it.
s: Pressure about 650 mb against about 1013 mb at the coast, so thinner air
Less oxygen reaches the lungs and blood; the body works harder
She can expect to feel breathless, dizzy or tired
No pause means no chance to acclimatise, so the risk is greater
States what the chapter does not give: the time needed or a remedy

questions.q: True or False: Climbers feel dizzy at 5,000 m because the atmospheric pressure there is higher than on the plains, which crowds oxygen out of their lungs. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Atmospheric pressure is lower at height, not higher. The air is thinner, so there is less oxygen for the lungs to take in, and less oxygen in the blood makes the body work harder, which leaves people breathless, dizzy or tired.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: pressure is lower at height; thinner air gives less oxygen, which causes the dizziness

questions.q: After a night of snow, a few centimetres of snow lie in the funnel of the school's rain gauge. At the usual time Hari reads the empty-looking cylinder and logs '0 mm'. What does the chapter say about his entry?
questions.a: The chapter tells the student to let snow melt before taking the measurement, because snow is a form of precipitation and the depth of the water collected is the rainfall. His 0 mm is therefore wrong. A gauge is not limited to rain, and the reading is the depth of melted water, not the depth of snow.
o: It is wrong: the snow should have been allowed to melt and the depth of the water read
It is right: a rain gauge measures only rain, and snow is not precipitation
It is right: snow should be logged as a depth in centimetres in place of the reading
It is wrong: the gauge should have been brought indoors and read in the evening

questions.q: Pooja says, 'The pressure at the sea coast is always 1013 mb, so if a barometer by the sea shows 995 mb, the barometer must be faulty.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. 1013 mb is the normal value, around which the pressure usually lies. The chapter says pressure can drop dramatically near the coast and below 1000 mb indicates a depression, so 995 mb may be a genuine reading showing a low-pressure system.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'always'
1013 mb is the normal value, not a fixed one
995 mb is below 1000 mb and indicates a depression

questions.q:
A harbour office reads its barometer once a day at noon, while the next harbour reads it every three hours.
(a) Which office is better placed to notice a developing depression, and why?
(b) Name one group of people, other than forecasters, who would use pressure readings and say what they would do with them.
questions.a: (a) The office reading every three hours: a depression is a dramatic drop in pressure, and frequent readings show the fall and the moment it passes below 1000 mb, which one noon reading may miss. (b) Any one with its use, for example sailors or fishermen deciding whether to put to sea, pilots, or travellers to high places who need to know the air is thin.
s: Part (a): the three-hourly office, since frequent readings catch a fall below 1000 mb
Part (b): a user group with a sensible use

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fall of the barometer below 1000 mb at a coastal town warns of a possible storm.
Reason (R): Atmospheric pressure is lowest at the sea coast, so any coastal reading below 1013 mb is a depression.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression, which can sometimes develop into a storm or cyclone. R is false: the pressure is higher near the sea coast and lower as one goes up, and the depression mark is below 1000 mb, not below 1013 mb.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
At 6 p.m. the district weather office receives barometer readings from two fishing harbours. Harbour A read 1011 mb at 6 a.m., 1010 mb at noon and 1010 mb at 6 p.m. Harbour B read 1013 mb at 6 a.m., 1007 mb at noon and 1001 mb at 6 p.m. The office can ask only one harbour to keep its boats back tonight; each harbour's fleet earns about 2 lakh rupees on a sailing night, and the office's rule is to hold the fleet whose pressure is on course to go below the depression mark of the chapter by midnight.
(a) Which harbour's pressure is falling steadily, and by how much every six hours?
(b) At that rate, what will Harbour B read at midnight, and will it be below the depression mark?
(c) Which harbour should be asked to keep its boats back? Decide and justify, saying what a depression can become.
questions.a: (a) Harbour B, by 6 mb every six hours (1013, 1007, 1001); Harbour A has hardly changed (1 mb in twelve hours). (b) 1001 - 6 = 995 mb, below 1000 mb. (c) Harbour B: its pressure falls steadily and will be below 1000 mb at midnight, so a depression is developing, which can become a storm or even a cyclone and endanger the boats. Harbour A, at 1010 mb and almost steady, is nowhere near the mark, so asking it to stay back loses 2 lakh rupees for no reason; a candidate who picks A earns no mark for the decision.
s: Part (a): Harbour B, 6 mb every six hours
Part (b): 995 mb, below 1000 mb
Part (c): Harbour B by the rule and the trend (1); a depression can become a storm or cyclone, so the boats are at risk (1)

questions.q: During a descent from a high camp on a clear day, a mountaineer's barometer rises from 700 mb to 760 mb in two hours. What best explains the rise?
questions.a: Pressure is higher near the sea coast and lower as one goes up into the mountains, so descending raises the reading. A depression is a fall of pressure, a barometer measures pressure not temperature, and the coast has the higher pressure, not the lower.
o: She is coming down, where the air is thicker and the pressure higher
A depression is forming over the camp, and a depression raises the pressure
The barometer measures temperature, which rises as she goes down
The coast has lower pressure than the mountains, so she must be nearing the coast

questions.q: A coastal town's barometer shows 650 mb on a calm, ordinary day, and the observer says the pressure is normal for the coast. Show why this cannot be right.
questions.a: The normal pressure at the sea coast is around 1013 mb, and a pressure below 1000 mb already indicates a depression, so a calm, ordinary day cannot go with 650 mb, which is 363 mb below the normal. The chapter gives about 650 mb as the pressure at a very high place such as Khardung La, over 5600 m up, where the air is thin; so the reading is the figure of a high place, and at a coastal town it must come from a faulty instrument or reading.
s: Normal coast pressure is around 1013 mb; below 1000 mb is a depression
650 mb is 363 mb below normal, far from a calm day
650 mb is the figure of a very high place, so the reading is faulty

questions.q: Write a one-line bulletin for a coastal town on a showery but ordinary evening. It must contain one rain-gauge reading and one barometer reading, and the barometer reading must give no cause for a storm warning. (a) Give the rain-gauge reading with its unit. (b) Give the barometer reading with its unit and say why it needs no warning.
questions.a: For example: 'Rainfall 9 mm today; barometer 1010 mb.' (a) The rain-gauge reading is a depth in mm. (b) The barometer reading is in millibars and is near the sea-coast normal of around 1013 mb, not below 1000 mb, so it does not indicate a depression.
s: Part (a): a rain-gauge depth with the unit mm
Part (b): a barometer reading in mb at or above 1000 mb (near 1013), with the reason that it is not a depression

questions.q: Two trekkers describe their day. Tanu: 'At the camp my barometer showed 760 mb; on the ridge it showed 700 mb, and I felt breathless.' Ujwal: 'At the coast my barometer fell from 1012 to 992 mb in a day, yet I felt fine.' Which statement does the chapter support?
questions.a: Tanu's fall is the usual fall of pressure with height, and her breathlessness is explained by thinner air with less oxygen. Ujwal's fall at the coast is a dramatic drop, and 992 mb is below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression. The two falls have different causes, so one cannot stand for the other.
o: Tanu's fall comes from climbing; Ujwal's, at 992 mb, indicates a depression
Both falls come from climbing, since pressure falls only with height
Both falls indicate depressions, since each reading is lower than 1013 mb
Tanu's fall indicates a depression, and Ujwal's is only the effect of height

questions.q: The school's open ground, with its raised level platform, is booked for a fair for the whole month. The group must set the rain gauge at one of: (1) the vegetable garden between banana plants 3 m tall; (2) the school terrace, open to the sky but with a slightly sloping floor; (3) the top of the compound wall, open but 10 cm wide; (4) the lab verandah, which has a roof. Which site should they use, and what must they do to make it acceptable?
questions.a: The terrace: it is open to the sky, so nothing obstructs the rain. The garden's tall plants would obstruct the rain, the verandah roof would keep the rain out of the funnel, and the narrow wall top is where a gauge could topple. The terrace's slope must be dealt with, for example by standing the gauge on a level platform or stand, since the gauge must be on a flat surface that will not tilt.
s: Chooses the terrace
Rejects garden and verandah (obstruct rain) and wall top (may topple)
Fix for the slope: a flat, level stand so the gauge does not tilt

questions.q:
Class 7B kept a gauge on a flat, open platform for four weeks of seven daily readings each. The weekly totals were: Week 1, 14 mm; Week 2, 35 mm; Week 3, 7 mm; Week 4, 21 mm.
(i) What must the class have done about the site and about the time of reading?
(ii) Find the daily average for each week.
(iii) Which week was wettest, and by how many mm per day did its average exceed the average of the whole month?
(iv) A student says Week 3's low average shows the gauge failed. Give the chapter-based reason this does not follow, and one check she can make.
questions.a: (i) Placed the gauge in the open, away from obstructions, on a flat surface that cannot tilt or topple, and read it at the same time every day. (ii) 2, 5, 1 and 3 mm per day. (iii) Week 2, with 5 mm per day; the month's total is 77 mm over 28 days, an average of 2.75 mm per day, so Week 2 exceeded it by 2.25 mm per day. (iv) Rainfall varies from week to week, so a dry week is possible and the chapter asks students to comment on the variation; she can check that the gauge was open and level and the funnel was not blocked.
s: (i) open and flat site, same time daily
(ii) 2, 5, 1 and 3 mm per day
(iii) Week 2, 2.25 mm per day above the month's average of 2.75
(iv) rainfall varies, so a dry week is not proof of failure
(iv) a check: gauge open, level, funnel clear

questions.q:
Two gauges stand a few metres apart on the same terrace after one heavy shower. Zoya's gauge, on the sloping part of the floor, leans slightly and shows 8 mm; Yash's, on the flat part, stands upright and shows 12 mm. Zoya proposes to add 4 mm to her record every time.
(a) Whose reading does the chapter's rule favour, and why?
(b) Why can she not simply add 4 mm?
questions.a: (a) Yash's: the chapter says the gauge should be on a flat surface so that it does not tilt, and his follows that rule. (b) The chapter gives no way to know how far a tilt changes a reading, so a fixed correction of 4 mm is a guess; she should move the gauge to a flat surface and measure again.
s: Part (a): Yash's, since the gauge must be on a flat surface and not tilt
Part (b): no known size of the tilt error, so a fixed correction is a guess; re-site and re-measure

questions.q:
A farmer near Raichur keeps a rain gauge in the open middle of his field and reads it at 8 a.m. each day. In ten days it shows, in mm: 0, 12, 0, 8, 0, 0, 15, 5, 0, 10. The agriculture officer's advice is to sow only when the running total since his first reading reaches 60 mm, and the radio expects about 4 mm a day for the next three days. Seed worth 12,000 rupees that fails to sprout is lost entirely.
(a) What does the 15 mm reading tell us about the area?
(b) Find the total for the ten days, the average per day and the number of days with any rain, and say how far the total is from the officer's 60 mm.
(c) Decide whether to sow now or wait three days, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The depth of rainwater collected in the cylinder was 15 mm, so the area received 15 mm of rainfall that day. (b) The total is 0 + 12 + 0 + 8 + 0 + 0 + 15 + 5 + 0 + 10 = 50 mm, an average of 5 mm a day, with rain on 5 of the 10 days; the total is 10 mm short of 60 mm. (c) Wait three days: at about 4 mm a day the total would reach about 50 + 12 = 62 mm, which meets the officer's 60 mm, whereas sowing now breaks the advice and risks 12,000 rupees of seed. Sowing now does not earn the mark, since the measured total is short of the stated limit.
s: Part (a): the depth of water collected was 15 mm, so the area received 15 mm of rainfall
Part (b): total 50 mm, average 5 mm a day, 5 rainy days, 10 mm short of 60
Part (c): wait about three days (about 62 mm expected); sowing now breaks the officer's rule and risks the seed

questions.q: Meera argues, 'Kochi and Mangaluru are both on the coast, so they must have the same humidity, and there is nothing to measure.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says humidity depends on factors like temperature, wind, pressure and location, so two coastal towns need not match; to know for sure, the humidity of each is measured with a hygrometer. Nearness to the sea may suggest a higher humidity, but it is a guess until measured.
o: Location is only one of several factors, so the two towns must be compared by measuring each with a hygrometer
Nearness to the sea fixes the humidity, so any two coastal towns have the same reading
Humidity does not depend on location, so it can be found from the temperature alone
Humidity is measured only inland, since air near the sea is always saturated

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A wind vane has a rotating arm with a pointer at one end and a tail at the other, and its pointer turns in the direction of the wind even in a light breeze.
Statement 2: A wind sock is used only at airfields and never by industries.
Statement 3: Humidity depends on the wind alone, so two towns with the same wind must show the same humidity.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: similar socks are used in industries that release ash or gases. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says humidity depends on factors like temperature, wind, pressure and location, not on wind alone.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: An anemometer's meter counted 120 spins of the cups in a 2-minute period on Monday morning and 150 spins in a 3-minute period on Tuesday morning. Tuesday's count is higher. Which day had the stronger wind?
questions.a: The stronger the wind, the faster the rotation, so the rate matters, not the total over different periods. Monday: 120/2 = 60 spins a minute; Tuesday: 150/3 = 50 spins a minute. Monday's wind was stronger. Direction is not needed to compare speeds.
o: Monday, as 60 spins a minute is faster than 50 spins a minute
Tuesday, as 150 spins is more than 120 spins
Both days, as the cups spun for a whole number of minutes
Neither can be said, as the direction of the wind is not given

questions.q:
Between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. the cups of an anemometer on a pole spin faster, while the pointer of the wind vane on the same pole does not move. At 6 p.m. the wind, which had been blowing from the east, now blows from the north, and the cups spin at the same rate as before.
(a) Describe what happened to the wind between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.
(b) Describe what changed at 6 p.m., and say which of the two instruments shows it.
questions.a: (a) The wind became stronger (its speed rose) but its direction did not change. (b) The wind's direction changed, from east to north, while its speed stayed the same; the wind vane shows the change of direction, as its pointer turns, while the cups show only speed.
s: Part (a): speed up, direction unchanged
Part (b): direction changed with speed unchanged; the wind vane shows it

questions.q: A hygrometer gives six readings in one day: 22%, 35%, 41%, 63%, 79% and 85%. The number of readings that fall in the chapter's usual band for humid weather is ___.
Gopal says, 'A greater wind speed makes the soil dry faster, so a farmer should watch the anemometer; the wind direction tells him nothing about the rain.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says a greater wind speed will cause the soil to dry faster, so the speed from the anemometer does matter to a farmer. But it also says farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from, so direction does tell him something about the rain, and a wind vane gives it.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: greater speed dries the soil faster
What is wrong: farmers use direction to predict where rain may come from

questions.q: A student's hygrometer reads 78% at 6 a.m. and 55% at 2 p.m. in the same garden on the same day. She says the instrument must be broken. What does the chapter let you say?
questions.a: The chapter says humidity depends on factors like temperature, wind, pressure and location. These can change between morning and afternoon, so a change in the reading is not by itself a fault. It does not say humidity must stay constant or within one band, and 78% and 55% are both possible readings of natural air.
o: A change is not by itself a fault, since humidity depends on factors such as temperature and wind that change through the day
The instrument is faulty, since the garden's humidity must stay within one band all day
The instrument is faulty, since a reading below 60% cannot follow one above 60%
The change shows the wind has stopped, since humidity depends on wind alone

questions.q: True or False: A cloth wind sock beside a chimney that releases ash can show the factory which way the ash will drift, but it cannot give the speed of the wind in km/h. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. A wind sock is a wind vane, which shows the direction of the wind; similar socks are used in industries that release ash or gases. The speed in km/h is counted by an anemometer, whose meter records the spins of its cups.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a sock shows direction like any wind vane; speed in km/h comes from an anemometer

questions.q:
A school's anemometer meter counted spins over different periods on five mornings: Day 1, 90 spins in 3 minutes; Day 2, 140 in 4 minutes; Day 3, 100 in 2 minutes; Day 4, 75 in 3 minutes; Day 5, 120 in 5 minutes.
(i) Find the spins per minute on each day.
(ii) Rank the days from strongest to weakest wind.
(iii) By how many spins a minute does Day 1 exceed Day 4, and which of the two days had the stronger wind?
(iv) On which day would wet soil in a field dry fastest, and why?
(v) The farmer also wants to know where rain might come from. Which instrument and which feature of the wind does he need?
questions.a: (i) 30, 35, 50, 25 and 24 spins a minute. (ii) Day 3, Day 2, Day 1, Day 4, Day 5. (iii) 30 - 25 = 5 spins a minute; Day 1 had the stronger wind, since the stronger the wind, the faster the rotation. (iv) Day 3, because the stronger the wind the faster the rotation and a greater wind speed dries the soil faster. (v) A wind vane, for the wind's direction. Accept wind vane (or wind sock) for (v); an anemometer answer is wrong because it counts spins.
s: (ii) ranking Day 3, 2, 1, 4, 5
(iii) 5 spins a minute; Day 1 stronger
(iv) Day 3: strongest wind dries soil fastest
(v) wind vane, direction

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The pointer of a wind vane turns in the direction of the wind, even in a light breeze.
Reason (R): Farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter. R tells what farmers do with the direction; it does not say why the pointer turns (the wind pushes the tail), so R does not explain A.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A potter in Jaipur and a potter in Kochi both wrap a wet cloth round a clay pot of water to cool it. The Jaipur pot cools much more. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: When water evaporates it causes a cooling effect. In dry air water evaporates quickly, so the cooling is greater; in humid air, which already holds much water vapour, water evaporates slowly, so the cloth cools the pot less. The temperature of the cloth is not what decides it.
o: Jaipur's air is drier, so the water in the cloth evaporates faster and cools more
Kochi's air is drier, so the water in the cloth evaporates slower and cools less
Jaipur's air is more humid, so the cloth holds more water vapour and cools the pot
The two cloths differ only in temperature, since evaporation does not cool

questions.q:
Neha's travel note reads: 'Hot and sticky; the towel I washed last night is still damp this evening.' Her hygrometer log has two entries, 47% and 71%, and she forgot which belongs to this place.
(a) Which entry belongs to this place?
(b) Where does each entry stand against the chapter's usual dry and humid bands, and how does evaporation explain her note?
questions.a: (a) 71%. (b) 47% lies between the dry band (20% to 40%) and the humid band (60% to 80%), so it is in neither; 71% lies inside the humid band. When the air already holds much water vapour, water evaporates slowly, so the towel stays damp and sweat dries slowly, which feels sticky.
s: Part (a): 71%
Part (b): 47% in neither band, 71% in the humid band; slow evaporation in humid air explains the damp towel and stickiness

questions.q:
At a small airfield near Nashik the ground staff watch a cloth sleeve on a pole and a four-cup instrument on the roof. On Monday the meter showed an average of 40 spins a minute. At 8 a.m. on Tuesday it showed 60 spins a minute, and the sleeve pointed steadily towards the hills. The airfield's own rule is that a trainee's first solo take-off is stopped when the meter shows more than 50 spins a minute; for any other flight the duty pilot decides. Two flights are planned for 10 a.m.: the trainee's first solo take-off, for a licence test slot after which the next slot is three weeks away; and an air-ambulance flight that must reach Pune within 90 minutes because a patient's operation begins at noon.
(a) Which instrument shows the pilots the wind's direction, and at which two moments of a flight do they use it?
(b) By what percentage did the spin rate rise from Monday to Tuesday, and what does that mean for the airfield's rule?
(c) Decide what should happen to each of the two flights, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The wind sock, a wind vane; at take-off and at landing. (b) (60 - 40) / 40 = 50 per cent higher spin rate, so the wind became stronger (the stronger the wind, the faster the rotation). Tuesday's 60 spins a minute is above the airfield's limit of 50 for a first solo take-off.
