(c) Postpone the trainee: the airfield's own rule stops the take-off, and the cost is a three-week wait for the next test slot. Let the ambulance fly: the rule does not bar it, the duty pilot decides, the pilots know the wind direction from the sleeve, and the patient's deadline cannot move. Allowing the trainee to fly does not earn the mark, because it breaks the airfield's rule; the chapter itself gives no safe speed, so the limit used is the airfield's.
s: Part (a): wind sock (a wind vane); at take-off and at landing
Part (b): 50 per cent rise, stronger wind; 60 is above the rule's limit of 50
Part (c): trainee postponed under the rule (cost: three weeks); ambulance flies at the duty pilot's judgement

questions.q:
Match each need in Column I with the instrument that serves it in Column II.
Column I: 1. A factory must warn the houses on the side towards which its ash drifts   2. A farmer wants the afternoon wind speed in km/h to judge how fast his wet field will dry   3. A curator must show that gallery air stays in the dry band   4. A coastal office wants an early sign of a depression
Column II: (a) Hygrometer   (b) Barometer   (c) Wind sock   (d) Anemometer
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Ash drift needs the wind direction, shown by a wind sock (c); wind speed in km/h comes from an anemometer (d); humidity is read with a hygrometer (a); a fall of pressure below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression, is read on a barometer (b). The other pairings swap two of these. A wind sock is a wind vane; an anemometer would be wrong for item 1 because it does not show which way the ash drifts.

questions.q: A student's table shows three hygrometer readings in school: 24% in the library, 0% in a closed laboratory and 100% on a foggy morning. Show that exactly one of the three cannot be a genuine reading of natural air, and say why each of the other two can be.
questions.a: The 0% reading cannot be genuine: it would mean air containing no water vapour at all, which is impossible in natural conditions. 24% lies in the usual dry band of 20% to 40%, so it is possible. 100% means air saturated with water vapour, which is the top of the scale and can occur, as on a foggy morning.
s: 0% is impossible: no water vapour at all
24% is in the dry band, so possible
100% is saturated air, so possible

questions.q:
On a flat plain Town P's barometer reads 1011 mb and Town Q's reads 1005 mb.
(a) In which direction does the air move between them?
(b) Which instrument at Q would show that direction, and what would its pointer do?
questions.a: (a) Wind is the movement of air from high pressure to low pressure, so the air moves from P towards Q. (b) A wind vane (wind sock); its tail is pushed by the wind and the pointer turns in the direction of the wind.
s: Part (a): from P (higher pressure) towards Q (lower)
Part (b): wind vane; its pointer turns in the direction of the wind

questions.q: A tour guide wants two forecast lines for travellers. Line 1 must be for a place where wet clothes will dry slowest and sweating will cool least. Line 2 must be for a place where the opposite holds. Write each line with a humidity figure from the chapter's bands, and give the chapter's reason in one sentence.
questions.a: Line 1: for example 'Humidity 78%: the air is humid.' Line 2: for example 'Humidity 30%: the air is dry.' Reason: in humid air, which already holds much water vapour, water evaporates slowly, so clothes dry slowly and the cooling effect of evaporation is small; in dry air evaporation is quick, so clothes dry faster and sweat cools more.
s: Line 1 with a humidity figure in or above the humid band (60% or more)
Line 2 with a humidity figure in the dry band (20% to 40%)
Reason: evaporation is slow in humid air and quick in dry air, with its cooling effect

questions.q:
A museum in Thiruvananthapuram records the relative humidity in its gallery at noon: Monday 45%, Tuesday 58%, Wednesday 70%, Thursday 84%. It holds 21 old palm-leaf manuscripts and paper maps. The curator's rule is that the manuscripts must never be exposed to air above 60% relative humidity, the lower edge of the chapter's humid band. Option X: close the windows and run machines in the whole gallery to keep the air dry, about 1 lakh rupees a month. Option Y: sealed dry cabinets, each holding 10 items and costing 25,000 rupees once; visitor policy requires the museum to open them for 2 hours every day, including on days like Wednesday and Thursday.
(a) Which instrument gave the readings, and which of the four readings lie in the chapter's usual humid band?
(b) By how many percentage points did the humidity rise from Monday to Thursday?
(c) How many cabinets are needed, and what is their one-time cost?
(d) Which option should the museum choose? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) A hygrometer; only Wednesday (70%) lies in the 60% to 80% band (58% is below it and 84% above it). (b) 84 - 45 = 39 percentage points. (c) 21 items need 3 cabinets (10 + 10 + 1), costing 3 x 25,000 = 75,000 rupees. (d) Option X. Y is cheaper (75,000 rupees once against 1 lakh a month), but opening the cabinets for 2 hours every day lets in air of 70% on days like Wednesday and 84% on days like Thursday, both above 60%, so the curator's rule is broken on two of the four recorded days; X keeps the whole gallery dry. A candidate who chooses Y earns 1 of the 2 marks only if the cost saving is shown and the exposure on humid days is admitted.
s: Part (a): hygrometer; Wednesday only
Parts (b) and (c): 39 points; 3 cabinets, 75,000 rupees
Part (d): Option X, because Wednesday's 70% and Thursday's 84% exceed 60% when the cabinets are opened (2); Y with the saving shown and the exposure admitted (1)

questions.q:
On a day when the wind blew steadily from the east towards the west, a botanist found the winged seeds of a tree only on the west side of the parent tree, mostly within 20 m. A week earlier, on a day when the cups of the anemometer spun twice as fast, seeds of the same tree had landed up to 40 m away.
(a) Which feature of the wind decides the side on which the seeds land, and which feature decides how far they travel? Name the instrument for each.
(b) What would happen to the spread of the seeds on a day with no wind?
questions.a: (a) The direction decides the side (wind vane); the speed decides the distance (anemometer): the stronger the wind, the faster the cups spin and the farther the seeds are carried. (b) The seeds would fall close to the parent tree, since nothing carries them across the field.
s: Part (a): direction with the wind vane; speed with the anemometer
Part (b): with no wind the seeds fall close to the parent tree

questions.q: On a flat plain the wind is blowing from Town X towards Town Y. The barometer at Y reads 996 mb, and the hygrometer at Y reads 72%. A farmer near Y has a wet field. Using the chapter: (i) name the instrument that shows the wind's direction and the one that gives its speed in km/h; (ii) say what the movement of air tells us about the pressure at X compared with Y; (iii) say what the hygrometer reading at Y means for the drying of the wet field, using the humid band; (iv) say how the farmer can use the wind direction; (v) say what the chapter lets us claim about the drying of his field if the anemometer shows a high wind speed, and what it does not let us claim about rain.
questions.a: (i) A wind vane (or wind sock) shows the direction; an anemometer gives the speed in km/h. Accept wind vane or wind sock for direction; an anemometer answer is wrong because it counts spins. (ii) Wind is the movement of air from high pressure to low pressure, so X has the higher pressure, above 996 mb. (iii) 72% lies in the usual humid band of 60% to 80%, so water evaporates slowly and the wet field dries slowly. (iv) Farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from; with the wind from X, the farmer near Y looks towards X. (v) A greater wind speed will cause the soil to dry faster, so a high reading speeds the drying; the chapter does not say that rain will actually come, so the direction alone gives no certainty of rain.
s: (i) wind vane or wind sock for direction; anemometer for speed
(ii) X has the higher pressure, above 996 mb
(iii) 72% is in the humid band, so evaporation and drying are slow
(iv) direction helps predict where rain might come from; the farmer looks towards X
(v) high speed dries soil faster; rain is not certain from direction alone

questions.q: True or False: A village that has an Automated Weather Station no longer needs a weather forecast that is accurate to the hour, because the station already gives the village its weather information. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. An Automated Weather Station measures and records weather data on its own, but a forecast is a prediction: meteorologists study such data over long periods with scientific methods to predict how the weather will behave. Data about what the weather is doing are not the same as a prediction of what it will do, and the prediction is what lets people prepare.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the station records data; meteorologists study the data to predict, and the prediction is what lets people prepare

questions.q: A forecast issued at 6 a.m. on Monday says a cyclone will reach a district's coast at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, so the coastal area must be evacuated before it arrives. The district first needs 12 hours to mobilise its resources (vehicles and relief camps), and only then can the move begin; moving everyone takes 36 hours. What is the latest time at which the district can start mobilising for the move to finish by landfall?
questions.a: Landfall is 60 hours after the forecast. Working back from 6 p.m. on Wednesday: 36 hours of moving, and before that 12 hours of mobilising, 48 hours in all, gives 6 p.m. on Monday as the latest start. Starting at 6 a.m. on Tuesday leaves only 36 hours, so the move would end 12 hours after landfall; 6 a.m. on Monday also works but is not the latest; 6 p.m. on Tuesday leaves only 24 hours.
o: 6 p.m. on Monday
6 a.m. on Tuesday
6 a.m. on Monday
6 p.m. on Tuesday

questions.q:
A school's barometer log has readings taken on Monday at 8 a.m. and 9 p.m., on Wednesday at 2 p.m., on Thursday at 7 a.m. and on Saturday at 11 a.m.
(a) What fault in this log makes it weak for mapping and forecasting, according to the chapter?
(b) Write a reading schedule for a five-day week that removes the fault.
questions.a: (a) The readings were not taken at regular intervals; the chapter says readings taken at regular intervals help in mapping and forecasting. (b) For example: every day at 8 a.m. and 8 p.m., so that the gap between readings is the same each time.
s: Part (a): readings not at regular intervals
Part (b): a schedule with equal gaps, such as the same hours daily

questions.q:
Match each description in Column I with what it describes in Column II.
Column I: 1. Studies readings collected over long periods with scientific methods and tries to predict the weather after hours, days or weeks   2. Measures and records weather data at a glacial lake over 4800 metres up without anyone staying there   3. Mobilises resources, and may evacuate an entire coastal area, when a cyclone is expected   4. Brings several instruments together and has its readings taken at regular intervals
Column II: (a) Automated Weather Station   (b) Meteorologist   (c) Local government   (d) Weather station
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Predicting from long records is the work of a meteorologist (b); a self-operating station at a remote lake is an Automated Weather Station (a); mobilising resources and evacuating is the local government (c); an arrangement that brings instruments together and is read at regular intervals is a weather station (d). The other pairings swap two of these.

questions.q: A TV anchor says, 'Weather forecasts matter only to fishermen.' Which pair of examples from the chapter best answers her?
questions.a: Accurate predictions let local governments mobilise resources and prepare for disasters, and AWS data is used in fields like agriculture and aviation, so forecasts matter well beyond fishermen. The pairs about fishermen alone, about traditional signs alone, and about instruments alone do not answer her, since they say nothing about users other than fishermen.
o: Governments mobilising resources for disasters, and AWS data used in agriculture and aviation
Fishermen being warned about venturing out in their boats, and boats staying in harbour
Elders reading ants and frogs for coming rain, and pine cones closing in humid conditions
A rain gauge placed in an open area, and a barometer reading displayed in millibars

questions.q: Meenal says, 'Weather predictions only warn us about storms and cyclones, so they are of no use in a district that has no coastline.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says climate change makes extreme weather such as droughts, floods and cyclones more frequent, and it lists droughts and floods beside cyclones, so forecasts are not only about cyclones. Accurate predictions help local governments mobilise resources and prepare for any disasters, and Automated Weather Station data is used in fields like agriculture and aviation, which need not be coastal.
s: Verdict: No
Droughts and floods are also extreme weather that forecasts help with
Governments prepare for any disasters; AWS data serves agriculture and aviation

questions.q:
A hill school wants a weather station on a ridge that, in the monsoon months, can be reached only by a three-hour climb. A manual station would need an observer paid 18,000 rupees a month, who would be unable to reach the ridge on about 10 days of each monsoon month. An Automated Weather Station would cost about 3.4 lakh rupees once. The school will run the project for 18 months, and the project report is accepted only if it has a reading for every day of the 18 months. The town has promised to keep the station running for some years after that.
(a) What feature lets an Automated Weather Station keep recording on the days no observer can climb?
(b) What is the observer's total pay for 18 months and by how much is it more or less than the cost of the Automated Weather Station, and after how many months does the observer's pay overtake that cost?
(c) Which station should the school choose? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) It is self-operating: its sensors measure and record the weather data without human intervention. (b) 18 x 18,000 = 3,24,000 rupees, which is 16,000 rupees less than 3,40,000; 3,40,000 / 18,000 is about 18.9, so the observer's pay overtakes the cost during the 19th month, just after the project ends. (c) The Automated Weather Station. The report needs a reading for every day, and the observer cannot climb on about 10 days of each monsoon month, so the observer's record would have gaps; the AWS also becomes cheaper from the 19th month while the town keeps it running. The observer is 16,000 rupees cheaper over the 18 months, but that saving does not meet the report's rule; a candidate who picks the observer earns 1 of the 2 marks only if the 16,000 saving is shown and the data gaps are admitted.
s: Part (a): self-operating sensors, no human intervention
Part (b): 3,24,000 rupees; 16,000 less; overtakes during the 19th month
Part (c): AWS, because the report needs every day and the observer leaves gaps (2); observer with the 16,000 saving shown and the gaps admitted (1)

questions.q:
A cyclone is forecast to reach the coast of an Odisha district in 36 hours. The harbour barometer reads 988 mb and has fallen for the last six hours. 40 fishing boats with 6 fishermen on each are in the harbour, and about 9,600 villagers may have to be moved to relief camps. Moving everyone takes about 20 hours. If the move is ordered now, about 1,800 working adults will lose two working days at 400 rupees a day each. The collector can instead wait 12 hours for a firmer forecast, which may show that the cyclone will pass by; but his own rule is to wait only if at least 8 hours of margin would remain.
(a) Which element is dominant while a cyclone is moving, and what does the barometer reading of 988 mb indicate?
(b) Find the wage loss if the move is ordered now, and the time margin left if the collector waits 12 hours, and compare it with his rule.
(c) Should the collector order the move now or wait 12 hours? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Atmospheric pressure is dominant; a reading below 1000 mb indicates a depression, so 988 mb does. (b) 1,800 x 2 x 400 = 14,40,000 rupees; waiting leaves 36 - 12 - 20 = 4 hours of margin, which is below his 8-hour requirement. (c) Order the move now: the margin after waiting breaks the collector's own rule, and the pressure is already below the depression mark and falling; the cost accepted is 14.4 lakh rupees of lost wages. Waiting does not earn the mark, because 4 hours is less than the 8 hours he requires; the 240 fishermen (40 x 6) should be warned at once in either case.
s: Part (a): atmospheric pressure; below 1000 mb is a depression
Part (b): 14,40,000 rupees; 4 hours of margin, below the 8-hour rule
Part (c): order the move now, justified by the rule and the falling pressure, with the wage cost named
